body_text: « Back PDF Version Sarepta Therapeutics Appoints Michael Severino, M.D., Chief Executive Officer 07/27/26 8:30 AM EDT – Severino joins Sarepta’s Board of Directors – Doug Ingram to retire from Sarepta CAMBRIDGE, Mass.--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Jul. 27, 2026-- Sarepta Therapeutics, Inc. (NASDAQ:SRPT), the leader in precision genetic medicine for rare diseases, today announced the appointment of Michael Severino, M.D., as chief executive officer, effective July 28, 2026. Severino, who was previously CEO of Tessera Therapeutics, will also join Sarepta’s Board of Directors. Severino succeeds Doug Ingram, who is retiring and will serve the company in an advisory capacity until the end of 2026 to ensure a smooth transition. Severino brings more than 25 years of biopharmaceutical experience to Sarepta. Prior to Tessera, he served as Vice Chairman and President at AbbVie, where he was responsible for research and development and the corporate strategy office. During his tenure at AbbVie, he oversaw a rapid expansion of AbbVie’s pipeline and built critical new capabilities in areas such as genetics and genomics, computational biology, and precision medicine. Severino has made significant contributions to more than a dozen approved therapies including Rinvoq®, Skyrizi®, and Venclexta® and, under his leadership, AbbVie built leading franchises in hematologic oncology, immunology, and neuroscience. Over the course of his career, he has led the strategy behind the research, development, registration, and commercialization of novel agents across a wide range of therapeutic areas and built critical capabilities needed to lead in the era of rapidly advancing precision medicine. “It is a privilege to join Sarepta, the leader in precision genetic medicine for rare diseases, and a company driven by an extraordinary purpose: bringing innovative therapies, hope and possibility to patients and families facing serious and life-threatening diseases,” said Severino. “Throughout my career, I have focused on combining cutting edge science with drug development and commercialization expertise to improve the lives of patients. Sarepta’s unwavering commitment to patients and science resonates deeply with me, and I was very encouraged by the long-term data supporting our approved products, and the pre-clinical and clinical data from the siRNA pipeline programs and the potential for best-in-class treatments. I look forward to working with my new colleagues at Sarepta to continue to serve the Duchenne community and expand our reach.” “After a comprehensive search, which identified multiple experienced and attractive candidates, the Board is pleased to welcome Mike as Sarepta’s next chief executive officer. Over a distinguished 25-year career in biopharmaceuticals, Mike has demonstrated a combination of scientific depth, development expertise, and proven execution that consistently delivers results,” said M. Kathleen Behrens, Ph.D., Chairperson of Sarepta’s Board of Directors. “His industry experience, strategic vision and commitment to patients, coupled with having built industry-leading franchises across multiple therapeutic areas, give us great confidence as he works to build on Sarepta’s strengths and steer the company as it continues to advance promising science on behalf of patients.” “On behalf of Sarepta’s Board, we thank Doug for his outstanding leadership and many contributions to the company,” Behrens continued. “He has led Sarepta’s evolution into a leader in genetic medicine, guiding the Company through a period of meaningful growth and transformative milestones, including the approvals of two exon-skipping treatments and the first one-time gene therapy for Duchenne muscular dystrophy. Throughout his tenure, Doug remained deeply committed to patients, driving innovation with a sense of urgency and purpose that has shaped Sarepta’s culture and future. We are grateful for his service and wish him the best in retirement.” “Leading Sarepta has been the honor of my professional career,” said Ingram. “I am particularly pleased that Mike inherits a company with a great team, a portfolio of life-changing therapies, a pipeline with exceptional potential and the financial resources to advance that science independently and at scale. Together, we have already brought a better future to thousands of patients and I am confident that under Mike’s leadership, Sarepta will continue to push the boundaries of what is possible and deliver an even greater impact for the people we serve.” About Michael Severino, M.D. Dr. Severino was formerly Chief Executive Officer at Tessera and a CEO-Partner at Flagship Pioneering, roles he had held since 2022. He joined Tessera from AbbVie where he was Vice Chairman and President responsible for research and development and the corporate strategy office. Prior to joining AbbVie, Severino served in roles of increasing responsibility at Amgen, Inc., leading to his appointment as Senior Vice President, Global Development and Chief Medical Officer. As Senior Vice President, he oversaw the company’s clinical development efforts across all therapeutic areas, including oncology, inflammation, neuroscience, cardiovascular, and metabolic disorders. Prior to Amgen, Severino was a Senior Director at Merck & Co., Inc., where he was responsible for leading research in multiple areas, including clinical genomics, molecular profiling, and experimental medicine. In addition to Sarepta, Severino also serves on the Board of Directors for Avantor, Montai Health, Quotient Therapeutics, and Viatris. Severino earned his Bachelor of Science in Biochemistry from the University of Maryland, College Park, where he graduated summa cum laude and was a member of the Phi Beta Kappa Society. He earned his M.D. from the Johns Hopkins University and completed his residency and post-doctoral training at Massachusetts General Hospital and Harvard Medical School. About Sarepta Therapeutics Sarepta is on an urgent mission: engineer precision genetic medicine for rare diseases that devastate lives and cut futures short. We hold a leadership position in Duchenne muscular dystrophy (Duchenne) and are building a robust portfolio of programs across muscle, central nervous system, and cardiac diseases. From Idea to Launch: How to Build a Startup App Without Blowing Your Budget (2026)
summary: Building a startup app doesn't have to mean hiring a dev team or burning your runway. This 7-phase guide covers everything from idea validation to launch using no-code and AI tools to ship faster and spend less.
body_text: Embarking on the journey of startup app development can feel like navigating a vast, exciting, and sometimes intimidating landscape. From a spark of an idea to a thriving digital product, the path is paved with critical decisions and key milestones. This guide breaks down the entire startup app development process into manageable stages, covering 31 essential topics to help you build and launch your app with confidence. Whether you are a founder with a vision or part of an innovation team, understanding these concepts is the first step toward success. Let’s explore the lifecycle of startup app development. Phase 1: Strategy and The Big Idea Before you write a single line of code, you need a solid foundation. This initial phase is all about research, validation, and planning to ensure you are building the right product for the right people. Idea Validation Idea validation is the process of testing your app concept to prove a real market need exists before you invest significant time and money. Up to 90% of startups fail, and the top reason, cited in 42% of cases, is building something nobody wants. You can validate your idea with surveys, landing pages, or simple prototypes to gather feedback and confirm demand. Market Research Market research involves gathering information about your target market, industry, and customers. It provides the data backed insights needed to shape your app’s direction, helping you build on facts, not assumptions. A surprising 23% of organizations admit they lack a clear market research strategy, which means many founders operate on guesswork. Competitor Analysis Competitor analysis is about identifying and evaluating other apps that solve the same problem you aim to solve. By understanding their strengths, weaknesses, and pricing, you can find gaps in the market and define your unique value. As part of this process, review alternatives in your category. Companies that use competitive intelligence report 15% higher revenue growth rates on average. Target Audience Definition Instead of building for everyone, you must define your target audience. This means identifying the specific group of people most likely to use and benefit from your app. Creating detailed buyer personas is a common practice here. In fact, 71% of companies that exceed their revenue goals have documented customer personas. Value Proposition Definition Your value proposition is a clear, compelling statement explaining the core benefit your app provides. It answers the question: “Why should someone choose your app over others?” A strong value proposition is crucial, as 63% of consumers will switch to a competitor that offers a better one. Protecting Your App Idea While you are validating your concept, it is wise to consider how to protect your intellectual property. This can involve using non disclosure agreements (NDAs) when speaking with partners or contractors, understanding copyrights for your code and design, and considering patents for unique, non obvious inventions. Securing your idea early provides peace of mind as you move forward. Phase 2: The Blueprint for Your App With a validated idea and a clear strategy, it is time to design the blueprint. This phase covers the technical and design decisions that will shape your product. Feature Prioritization You cannot build everything at once. Feature prioritization is the process of deciding which features to build first. This is critical because studies show that 64% to 80% of software features are rarely or never used. Focusing on core functionalities for your initial release helps you launch faster and avoid wasting resources. Platform Selection Platform selection involves deciding where your app will run: on iOS, Android, the web, or a combination. This choice affects your audience reach and development stack. With Android holding roughly 72% of the global smartphone market and mobile devices accounting for over 62% of website traffic, choosing the right platform is a key strategic decision. Development Approach Selection Here you decide how to build your app. Will you use a traditional coding approach or a modern visual development platform? Agile methodologies, which emphasize iterative progress, are now used by 71% of companies. Furthermore, the rise of powerful tools is changing the game. Gartner predicts that by 2025, 70% of new applications will be built using low code or no code platforms. Platforms like WeWeb are at the forefront of this shift, blending AI and no code to help you build production grade applications faster and more efficiently. UI and UX Design User Interface (UI) and User Experience (UX) design are about making your app visually appealing, intuitive, and enjoyable to use. Good design is not just a luxury, it is a necessity. Every $1 invested in UX can yield a return of up to $100. A poor user experience can drive away customers, while a great one builds loyalty. ‍ "With WeWeb, we were truly able to achieve a pixel-perfect representation of our complex Figma designs." - Mike Coulbourn, Founder & CEO of SkipMatrix . Wireframing and Prototyping Wireframing and prototyping are essential steps to visualize and test your app’s layout and flow before development. A wireframe is a simple structural sketch, while a prototype is an interactive model. Fixing a design issue during the prototype phase can be 100 times cheaper than fixing it after launch. Technology Stack Selection Your technology stack is the set of programming languages, frameworks, and tools used to build your app. For years, JavaScript has been the most commonly used programming language, with Python also being a popular choice for its simplicity and power. The right stack depends on your app’s specific needs for performance, scalability, and your team’s expertise. App Architecture Design App architecture is the high level blueprint of your app’s technical structure. It defines how components interact, how data flows, and whether you will use a monolithic or microservices based approach. A good architecture is vital for scalability and maintenance, which is why an estimated 77% of organizations have adopted microservices to build more flexible and robust systems. Phase 3: Building and Perfecting Your Product This is where your vision starts to become a tangible product. The development phase focuses on building, testing, and ensuring quality. MVP Development MVP stands for Minimum Viable Product. It is a version of your app with just enough features to be usable by early customers who can then provide feedback for future development. This approach, used by successful companies like Dropbox, allows you to launch quickly, learn from real users, and avoid building features nobody wants. You can build a working MVP in days with a no code platform like WeWeb using starter templates , allowing you to test your riskiest assumptions with minimal investment. Testing and Quality Assurance Testing and Quality Assurance (QA) are processes for finding and fixing bugs to ensure your app is reliable and secure. Software failures can be incredibly costly, with one report estimating they cost companies $1.7 trillion in a single year. Continuous testing throughout the development cycle is a core part of modern startup app development. Phase 4: Go to Market and Launch With a polished product in hand, it is time to introduce it to the world. A successful launch requires careful planning and execution. "Time to build and time to market is really effective with WeWeb." - Elyse Holladay, Product Lead at Hello Generalist Developer Account Setup To publish your app on platforms like Apple’s App Store or the Google Play Store, you first need to set up a developer account. Apple’s program costs $99 per year, while Google Play requires a one time $25 fee. This is a necessary administrative step to gain access to the distribution channels where users will find your app. App Store Submission App store submission involves preparing your app’s listing (title, description, screenshots) and submitting the build for review. Apple’s review process is notoriously thorough, with reports suggesting that around 40% of initial submissions are rejected for not meeting guidelines. A polished submission is key to getting approved and making a good first impression. Launch Strategy A launch strategy is your plan for releasing your app to maximize impact and user adoption. This includes timing your launch, generating pre launch buzz with a landing page, and reaching out to press or influencers. A well coordinated launch can result in two to three times more downloads in the first week. Marketing and User Acquisition After launch, you need an ongoing strategy for marketing and user acquisition to attract new users. This can include paid ads, content marketing, social media engagement, and referral programs. A lack of a solid marketing strategy is cited as a key reason for failure by 22% of startups. App Store Optimization (ASO) App Store Optimization, or ASO, is like SEO for app stores. It is the process of optimizing your app’s listing to rank higher in search results. Since about 65% of all downloads come directly from searches on the App Store, ASO is one of the most effective ways to drive organic installs. Phase 5: The Business of Your App A great app also needs a sustainable business model behind it. This phase covers the financial and operational aspects of your startup. Monetization Model Your monetization model is how your app generates revenue. Common models include paid downloads, freemium (free with in app purchases), subscriptions, and advertising. Today, the freemium and subscription models dominate, accounting for nearly all revenue generated on the app stores. Funding Option Funding is the capital you need to build and grow your app. Options range from bootstrapping (self funding) to raising money from angel investors or venture capital (VC) firms. While VC funding gets a lot of attention, it is quite rare, with less than 1% of startups receiving it. Many founders start by bootstrapping or raising a small round from friends and family. Budget Planning Budget planning involves forecasting and allocating the financial resources needed for your project. It is crucial to be realistic, as a McKinsey study found that large IT projects run 45% over budget on average. A well planned budget acts as your financial roadmap and helps prevent you from running out of money unexpectedly. Cost Estimation Cost estimation is the process of predicting the financial cost of building your app. This is notoriously difficult, with industry data showing that only about 31% of projects come within 10% of their original budget. Breaking the project into smaller tasks and getting expert opinions can help you create a more accurate forecast. Team Hiring and Outsourcing You will need to decide whether to build an in house team or outsource development to an agency or freelancers. Outsourcing is often chosen to reduce costs, with 59% of businesses citing it as a primary reason. The right choice depends on your budget, timeline, and long term vision for your startup app development project. Development Timeline Planning A development timeline is your schedule for building and launching the app. It maps out all major phases, tasks, and milestones. Since only about a third of projects are delivered on time, it is wise to build buffer time into your plan to account for unexpected delays. “I built W4.0 on my own. Aside from a bit of help with algorithms, I did it all. That kind of speed and independence was game-changing.” - Jon Adair, co-founder & CTO at W4.0 Phase 6: Growth and The Long Game Launching your app is just the beginning. Long term success depends on continuous improvement, user engagement, and support. Analytics and Measurement Setup You cannot improve what you do not measure. Setting up analytics tools like Google Analytics or Mixpanel, or routing events via Google Tag Manager , allows you to track user behavior, identify drop off points, and make data driven decisions. Companies that adopt this approach are often 5% to 6% more productive and profitable. Retention Strategy A retention strategy focuses on keeping users engaged and coming back. This is vital, as it can be 5 to 25 times more expensive to acquire a new customer than to retain an existing one. Tactics include a great onboarding experience, push notifications, in-app messaging with Intercom , and personalization to create a sticky product. Post Launch Iteration and Support After launch, the real work begins. Post launch iteration involves continuously improving your app based on user feedback and analytics. This cycle of releasing updates, fixing bugs, and providing customer support is what turns a good app into a great one that stands the test of time. Phase 7: Security and Compliance In today’s digital world, protecting your users and your business is non negotiable. Security and Data Privacy Building a secure app that protects user data is essential for maintaining trust. This includes everything from secure logins and data encryption to following secure coding practices and having a Data Processing Agreement (DPA) in place with key vendors. The average cost of a data breach was $4.24 million in 2021, a figure that could be fatal for a startup. Regulatory Compliance Regulatory compliance means adhering to laws like GDPR in Europe and CCPA in California. These regulations govern how you handle personal data, and non compliance can lead to massive fines. For example, fines under GDPR can be up to 4% of a company’s global annual turnover. Staying compliant is a critical part of operating a responsible and sustainable business. Ready to bring your own app idea to life? Discover how you can accelerate your startup app development with WeWeb , and see real apps built with WeWeb . Frequently Asked Questions 1. What is the first step in startup app development? The very first step is idea validation. Before anything else, you need to research and confirm that there is a genuine market need for the problem your app intends to solve. 2. How much does it cost to develop an app for a startup? Costs vary widely based on complexity, features, and the development approach. A simple Minimum Viable Product (MVP) might cost anywhere from $10,000 to $50,000, while a more complex application can run into hundreds of thousands of dollars. 3. How long does startup app development typically take? The timeline also varies. A simple MVP can often be built in 2 to 4 months. A full featured app with complex backend systems can take 6 to 12 months or longer. Using modern tools can significantly speed up this process. 4. Can I build an app with no coding knowledge? Yes. No code and low code platforms have made startup app development more accessible than ever. Tools like WeWeb provide visual editors and AI assistance that allow you to build powerful, scalable web applications without writing traditional code. 5. How do I choose between iOS, Android, and a web app? The choice depends on your target audience and budget. If your users are primarily in North America and you want to monetize effectively, iOS might be a good start. For global reach, Android is essential. A web app offers the broadest accessibility across all devices without requiring an app store download. 6. What is the most important factor for an app’s success? While many factors contribute, achieving product market fit is arguably the most important. This means building a solution that effectively solves a real problem for a well defined audience, leading to high user retention and organic growth.

title: Management reporting: how to build a monthly management report
summary: Management reporting is the recurring internal pack leaders use to run the business. Here is what to include, how often to run it, and how to automate it.
body_text: Management reporting is the recurring internal report that leadership uses to run the business between planning cycles. It combines financial results, operational metrics, and short written commentary into a single package, usually monthly, so the people accountable for the company can see what happened, why it happened, and what to do next. It is different from statutory financial reporting, which exists to satisfy accounting standards and outside stakeholders. A management report exists to drive internal decisions. This guide is for founders, finance leads, heads of operations, and anyone who has inherited the job of assembling a monthly management pack. It covers what belongs in the report, how the pieces fit together, how often to run it, who should own it, and how to move from a hand-built spreadsheet to something that assembles itself. TL;DR Management reporting is the recurring internal pack that leaders use to run the business. Financial reporting is for compliance and outsiders; management reporting is for decisions. A useful monthly pack has six parts: a headline scorecard, financials with variance, the growth engine, operational health, cash and runway, and written commentary. The written commentary is the part that turns numbers into decisions. Skip it and you have a data dump, not a report. Run it monthly for the full pack, with a lighter weekly or biweekly pulse on a few live metrics. Ownership belongs to one person, usually finance or ops. Automating the data assembly is what makes a single owner sustainable. What is management reporting? Management reporting is the practice of producing regular internal reports that measure how the business is performing against its plan and its goals. The output is often called the management pack, management accounts, or the monthly report. It typically includes the profit and loss statement, cash position, a set of operational KPIs, and a written narrative explaining the results. The distinction that matters is audience and purpose. Statutory financial statements follow GAAP or IFRS and are built for tax authorities, auditors, lenders, and investors. Management reports follow whatever structure helps the leadership team make decisions. They can mix accrual financials with cash metrics, include non-financial operational data, and present numbers in whatever cut is most useful, such as by product line, region, or customer segment. A good management report answers three questions in order: Where are we against plan? Why are we ahead or behind? What are we going to do about it? If a report answers the first question but not the second and third, it is a scorecard, not a management report. Management reporting vs board reporting vs financial reporting These three overlap enough that people use the terms interchangeably, but they serve different readers and cadences. Attribute Management reporting Board reporting Financial reporting Primary audience Internal leadership team Board of directors Auditors, tax, lenders, investors Purpose Run the business Govern and advise Compliance and disclosure Cadence Monthly (plus weekly pulse) Quarterly Quarterly and annual Detail level High, operational Curated, strategic Standardized, prescribed Standards Internal, flexible Internal, board-driven GAAP or IFRS Includes commentary Yes, detailed Yes, framed as narrative Notes to accounts only Includes operational KPIs Yes Selected No The management report is usually the source the others draw from. The board reporting dashboard is a curated, higher-altitude version of the same numbers, produced quarterly. The statutory accounts are the formal financial subset, cleaned and standardized. If your management reporting is solid, the board pack and the financials become extracts rather than separate projects. What belongs in a monthly management report Most companies are well served by six sections. The order follows how a leadership team actually reads performance: the outcome first, then the money, then the engine producing the money, then operations, then survival, then the story that ties it together. 1. Headline scorecard One screen, readable in under a minute. Three to seven metrics the company is being run against this period, each shown with the actual value, the target or plan, and the trend. For a B2B SaaS company this is usually revenue or ARR, net new ARR, gross margin, net revenue retention, and runway. Do not get creative here. Use the metrics leadership already agreed to. 2. Financials with variance The profit and loss statement compared against budget, with the variances that matter called out. This is where budget vs actual variance analysis lives. Show revenue, cost of goods sold, gross margin, operating expenses by function, and operating income or net loss. Flag every line that is materially off plan and explain it in the commentary. A variance without an explanation is noise. 3. Growth engine The metrics that explain why revenue moved: pipeline, new bookings, churn and contraction, expansion, conversion rates, and customer acquisition cost against lifetime value. This section answers whether the top line is healthy or borrowed from the future. A month can hit its revenue number while the pipeline that feeds next quarter quietly collapses. This is where you catch that. 4. Operational health The non-financial metrics specific to how the business runs. For a product company this might be active users, activation rate, and support load. For a services company it might be utilization and delivery margin. For operations-heavy businesses it might be fulfillment time or error rates. Pick the three to five operational metrics that predict future financial results. 5. Cash and runway Cash on hand, monthly burn, and runway in months at the current rate. For early-stage companies this is often the single most important section. Include a short cash forecast if your burn is variable. Investors and boards will forgive a missed revenue target far more readily than a surprise about runway. 6. Written commentary The part that turns the pack into a report. Two to four paragraphs, written by the report owner, explaining what happened, why, and what the team is doing about it. Good commentary is specific: “Net new ARR came in 18 percent under plan because two enterprise deals slipped to next quarter; both are verbally committed and expected to close by the 15th.” That sentence is worth more than any chart in the pack. Leave out anything that does not drive a decision. A management report is not a place to prove how much you can measure. If a metric has never once changed what leadership did, drop it. How often should you run management reporting? Run two cadences at different depths. The full monthly pack ships a few business days after the accounting close, once actuals are final. Five to ten business days after month end is typical, and faster is better. A pack that lands three weeks into the next month is a history lesson, not a decision tool. A lighter weekly or biweekly pulse covers the handful of live metrics that can move meaningfully within a month: pipeline, bookings, cash, and any leading operational metric. This pulse does not need commentary or a formal layout. It can be a live dashboard link or a short automated summary. The point is to catch problems between monthly reports, not to duplicate them. Quarterly, the management report rolls up into the executive dashboard and board pack, which take a longer view and drop the month-to-month detail. Who should own the management report? One person owns the management report. On small teams it is usually the founder or the head of finance. As the company grows it moves to a finance manager, controller, or head of operations. Distributed ownership, where each department submits its own section with no editor, produces packs that contradict each other and take forever to assemble. The owner is responsible for three things: the numbers being right and consistently defined, the pack shipping on schedule, and the commentary being honest. They are not responsible for producing every number by hand. That is what the data layer is for. Company stage Typical owner Cadence Assembly method Pre-seed to seed Founder Monthly Spreadsheet Seed to Series A First finance or ops hire Monthly + weekly pulse Spreadsheet plus live dashboards Series A to B Finance manager or controller Monthly + weekly pulse BI tool connected to source systems Series B and beyond FP&A or finance team Monthly, weekly, ad hoc Automated pipeline plus BI layer From spreadsheet to automated: a maturity ladder The reason management reporting eats so many hours is that the data lives in different places: the accounting system holds financials, the billing or CRM system holds revenue detail, and the production database holds product and operational metrics. Assembling the pack means pulling from all of them and reconciling. Here is how teams usually progress. Level 1, manual spreadsheet. Someone exports CSVs from each system every month and pastes them into a template. This works at the earliest stage and nowhere else. It is slow, error-prone, and the person who built it becomes a single point of failure. Level 2, connected spreadsheet. The spreadsheet pulls from source systems through connectors or a live sync, so the numbers refresh without copy-paste. Better, but spreadsheets still break under version sprawl and stop scaling once multiple people touch them. Level 3, BI tool on live data. A business intelligence tool connects directly to the accounting system, the warehouse, and the production database, and the report sections become saved dashboards. Financials, growth metrics, and operational health all read from the same governed source. The owner spends their time on commentary and analysis instead of assembly. This is where establishing a single source of truth pays off, because every metric has one agreed definition. Level 4, automated distribution. The pack assembles and delivers itself on a schedule. Dashboards refresh after the close, and scheduled reports push the relevant views to the right people, leaving only the written commentary for a human. Most companies do not need to reach this level to feel the benefit; the jump from Level 1 to Level 3 is the one that returns days per month. A modern BI tool like Basedash fits at Level 3 and above. It connects to a production database or warehouse, lets non-technical teammates explore the numbers and ask follow-up questions without waiting on the finance owner, and turns the recurring report into a set of live views rather than a monthly rebuild. The value is not fancier charts; it is that the owner stops spending the first week of every month reconciling exports. Common mistakes in management reporting Reporting everything. A pack with sixty metrics hides the five that matter. Every metric should earn its place by having changed a decision at least once. Numbers without commentary. Charts show what happened. Only the written narrative explains why and what comes next. Boards and leadership teams remember the commentary, not the pie chart. Inconsistent definitions. If “active customer” or “gross margin” means something different this month than last, the report loses trust fast. Define each metric once and reuse the definition everywhere. Shipping late. A report that arrives three weeks after month end cannot change anything about that month. Speed of delivery is a feature, not a nicety. One person, one spreadsheet, no backup. When the pack lives entirely in one person’s head and one fragile file, it breaks the month they are on vacation. Automating the data layer is what makes single ownership safe. When a lightweight approach is enough Not every company needs a formal management pack. If you are pre-revenue or a very small team, a shared dashboard with cash, burn, and a couple of leading metrics, reviewed weekly, is plenty. Formal monthly reporting earns its keep once you have a real budget to track against, a leadership team that needs a shared view, or investors who expect regular updates. The signal to formalize is usually one of these: you have raised a priced round, you have more than one department making spending decisions, or you have caught a problem too late because nobody was looking at the right number. When any of those happen, it is time to build the six-section pack and pick an owner. FAQ What is the difference between management reporting and financial reporting? Financial reporting produces standardized statements under GAAP or IFRS for external parties such as auditors, tax authorities, and lenders. Management reporting produces internal reports built to help leadership make decisions. Management reports can mix accrual and cash figures, include operational metrics, and use any structure that is useful, whereas financial statements follow a prescribed format. What should a monthly management report include? A useful monthly pack has six parts: a headline scorecard of three to seven goal metrics, the profit and loss statement with variance against budget, growth-engine metrics such as pipeline and retention, operational health metrics, cash and runway, and a written commentary explaining the results. The commentary is the part that turns data into decisions. How soon after month end should the report go out? Aim for five to ten business days after the accounting close, and faster if you can. A pack that lands three weeks into the following month describes history the team can no longer act on. Speed matters more than polish. What are management accounts? Management accounts are the financial portion of a management report: an internal profit and loss statement, balance sheet, and cash flow prepared for leadership rather than for statutory filing. They are often produced monthly and paired with operational KPIs and commentary to form the full management pack. Do you need a BI tool for management reporting? Not at the earliest stage, when a spreadsheet is fine. Once data lives across an accounting system, a billing or CRM system, and a production database, a BI tool that connects to all of them removes the monthly export-and-reconcile work and lets the owner focus on analysis and commentary instead of assembly. How is management reporting different from board reporting? Board reporting is a curated, quarterly, strategic view for directors. Management reporting is a more detailed, monthly, operational view for the internal leadership team. The management report is usually the source the board pack is built from, so strong management reporting makes board reporting faster.

title: Hagerty Indexes Trend Upwards Despite a Picky Market

body_text: The Hagerty Price Guide Indexes—first published in 2009—are a series of stock market-style indexes that average the condition #2 (“excellent”) values of representative vehicles, or “component” cars, from a particular segment. These indexes are updated quarterly and provide an overview of how these segments of the collector car market are performing overall, as well as relative to each other. The year is more than halfway done, and it’s been a wild ride so far. Some areas of the market have fared well while others have cooled gently, all while being overshadowed by the explosive growth of modern exotics. While things tend to quiet down in the couple months leading up to the Monterey auctions in August, seven of our 11 market indexes showed growth, with none of our other indexes declining. Yet again, Supercars are the bright spot in the market with broad and sustained growth beyond what anyone could’ve expected a year ago. While many of our other indexes ( British Cars , Ferrari , American Muscle , German Cars , 1950s American , RADindex , and Japanese ) posted gains, many can be explained away by big increases in a handful of cars. While the Hagerty Market Rating still sits in “flat” territory, the market indexes and their component cars show the more nuanced nature of the collector car world. Anyone looking for clarity in this wild market may be looking for some time more. Blue Chip Index Aston Martin The Hagerty “Blue Chip” Index of the automotive A-List is a stock market-style index that averages the values of 25 of the most sought-after collectible automobiles of the post-war era. Following last quarter’s 2% increase, Hagerty’s Blue Chip Index has remained rock steady heading into the summer. Of the 25 component cars, nearly 70% of them tracked no movement with the rest showing mixed results. Late spring through early summer is typically a slow time for Blue Chip collectors, and this year is no exception. Upward movement was confined to just three cars. The Aston Martin DB5 jumped 17%, the 1965 Shelby GT350 gained 12% after last quarter’s bump, and the Shelby Cobra 427 notched a 4% increase. Balancing these increases out were five cars losing value: the Lancia Aurelia Spider America (-12%), Bentley S1 Continental (-1%), Tucker 48 (-3%), Rolls-Royce Silver Cloud (-3%), and BMW 507 (-1%). Heading into August, this segment will be the one to watch with the auctions in Monterey, California setting the tone for expensive, top tier vintage collector cars for the remainder of the year. British Car Index Hagerty Marketplace The Hagerty Index of British Cars is a stock market-style index that averages the values of 10 of the most iconic British sports cars from the 1950s-70s. Following last quarter’s 6% dip, Hagerty’s British Car Index pulled off a 2% recovery, ending six consecutive quarters of downward movement. Of the 10 component cars, nearly half posted gains, while just three continued to retreat in value. Leading the pack was the MGA 1600 which posted a remarkable gain of 10%, closely followed by the Jaguar E-Type and Triumph TR3A, which gained 7%. Meanwhile, the Triumph TR6 posted a 12% loss, followed by modest drops by the Austin-Healey 100M Le Mans (-2%) and Jaguar XK120 Roadster (-1%). For the past four years, the British Car Index has been trending downward, facing headwinds from a shifting market. While the recent gain does stir some optimism, past trends suggest further monitoring of this market for signs of true recovery. Ferrari Index Broad Arrow The Hagerty Ferrari Index is a stock market-style index that averages the values of 13 of the most sought-after street Ferraris of the 1950s-70s. Hagerty’s Ferrari Index saw a sizable increase this past quarter, with a 9% jump. But this major shift came mostly thanks to one component car, the 250 LM. The rare (32 built) racer’s staggering 29% jump in value comes at the news of a private treaty sale well above our posted numbers in the price guide, putting this model into low-end 250 GTO territory in terms of value. Outside of the 250 LM, only three other component cars saw changes. The 365 GTB/4 Daytona Coupe gained 6%, while the 330 GTC and 410 Superamerica adjusted downward by 2% and 1%, respectively. Otherwise, Enzo-era Ferraris have remained steady for the most part. The upcoming Monterey auctions are historically a good test for this segment, so it will be important to keep a close eye on the auctions for a true gauge of the classic Ferrari market. American Muscle Car Index Mecum The Hagerty Index of American Muscle Cars is a stock market-style index that averages the values of the rarest and most sought-after muscle cars. Following a quiet beginning to the year, Hagerty’s Muscle Car Index enjoyed a 2% increase as summer heated up. This follows another flurry of activity in the late spring and although fewer component cars saw movement from the previous quarter (eight instead of 11), the ones that increased did so by strong amounts. The clear driver of this quarter’s movement was the staggering 75% jump by the American Motors AMX Super Stock. These are very rarely seen, and a strong sale of one this past quarter prompted a large adjustment. In addition, big increases were posted by the 1970 Chevelle SS LS6 (15%), 1965 Shelby GT350 (12%), and 1970 Oldsmobile 4-4-2 W-30 (10%). These jumps were only slightly tempered by the 1970 Buick GS455’s 18% loss, followed by moderate drops for the 1965 GTO, 1968 Shelby GT500 KR and 1969 Mustang Boss 429. Despite the index’s overall gain, muscle cars remain a mixed bag as the segment looks to find clear direction amongst changing market conditions. German Car Index Broad Arrow The Hagerty Index of German Cars is a stock market-style index that averages the values of 21 of the most sought-after cars from BMW, Mercedes-Benz, and Porsche from the 1950s-70s. Hagerty’s German Car Index clawed back last quarter’s 1% loss with an equally modest 1% gain. Of the 13 component cars, the three gainers managed to overpower the five losses we tracked. The main contributor to the jump was the earliest Porsche 356s produced at the Gmünd, Austria factory, which increased by 13% following years of no movement, as well as the 18% bump to the 1965 Porsche 356C 1600 SC Coupe. The 8% decreases to the 1967 Porsche 911S Targa and Mercedes-Benz 190SL, as well as more modest decreases across the board, helped temper the gain. This is another case where one occasional move for a rare car changes the entire game. The underlying trend is that older German collectors are slowly cooling while new models are exploding in value. 1950s American Car Index Mecum The Hagerty Index of 1950s American Classics is a stock market-style index that averages the values of 19 of the most sought-after collectible American automobiles of the 1950s. Hagerty’s 1950s American Car Index came in with a 1% gain, erasing last quarter’s 1% loss, but this segment still has ground to claw back after a year of consistent decreases. Of the 19 component cars, five gained in value while another five lost value over the previous quarter. The main drivers of this increase were the 20% increase by the 1958 Studebaker Golden Hawk and the 10% bump to the 1953 Hudson Hornet. Neither car is a common sight in the market, so further growth of this magnitude is unlikely. Meanwhile, the 12% decrease by the 1950 Oldsmobile Series 88 Wagon and the 8% loss to the 1956 Ford Fairlane Sunliner and 1957 Fairlane Skyliner show that more common entries are showing signs of weakness. While it has long been expected that 1950s American cars will struggle as younger and younger enthusiasts enter the hobby, the real picture is much more nuanced with a clear direction yet to materialize. Affordable Classics Index Mecum The Hagerty Index of Affordable Classics is a stock market-style index that averages the values of 13 undervalued cars, priced around $40,000, from the 1950s-70s. Hagerty’s Affordable Classics Index entered the second half of the year tracking no movement, following the previous quarter’s 1% loss. Lack of index movement doesn’t indicate lack of movement in individual vehicles, though. Of the 13 component cars, four gained in value this past quarter while two decreased. The notable gainers included the Volkswagen Beetle and Karmann Ghia, which increased by 5% and 7%, respectively, as well as the Datsun 240Z (5%), MGB (4%), and Studebaker Lark (2%). Downward movement was spread across the Triumph TR6 (-12%), 1949 Buick Roadmaster Sedanet (-10%), and Studebaker Avanti (-3%). Some traditionally “affordable” classics have grown out of reach over the past few years, but some have also started to come back down to earth. Expect this trend to continue as some of the more mainstream parts of the market continue to soften. RADindex Brandan Gillogly The Hagerty RADindex is a stock market-style index that averages the values of 21 collectible vehicles from the 1980s and 1990s. Hagerty’s RADindex keeps chugging along, and posted up another small increase of 1.5% this past quarter. The new all-time high comes at the hands of a number of small increases across seven of the 21 component cars, with no vehicles losing value. The biggest gainers were the 1987 Buick GNX and Lancia Delta Integrale, which both increased by 6%. Smaller increases came from the Delorean DMC-12 (3%), third gen Camaro Z28 (2%), C4 Corvette ZR-1 (2%), E30 M3 (1%), and Acura NSX (1%). Slow and steady wins, and the RADindex keeps delivering. This collection of next generation collectors is as steady and sure as they come, and should enjoy a bright future as market interests continue to shift towards later collectors. Truck and SUV Index Mecum The Hagerty Truck and SUV Index is a stock market-style index that averages the values of 19 collectible trucks and SUVs from the 1940s to the 1990s. Of our newly added indexes, Hagerty’s Truck Index is the only one that has tracked no meaningful movement. A lack of overall movement, however, does not mean there was no activity. Of the 19 component trucks, 10 saw movement with a half moving down while the other five increased. The clear winners were the 1984–89 Toyota Pickup and 1948–52 Ford F-Series increasing by 14% and 12%, respectively, while the 1966–77 Ford Bronco’s surprising 14% loss offset the gains. The mixed bag of movement clearly shows that buyers are getting increasingly picky about what they’re buying and how much they’re willing to shell out. Discernment and restraint is a positive in the long term, something seemingly absent in some other areas of the market at the moment. Japanese Vehicle Index Subaru The Hagerty Japanese Vehicle Index is a stock market-style index that averages the values of 19 collectible Japanese vehicles from the 1960s to the 2010s. After nearly a year of no movement, Hagerty’s Japanese Index roared to life increasing by 11%. This increase was largely driven by a spike in value of the Lexus LFA, which jumped by 18%, riding the wave of the modern exotic market. Coming back to earth, five additional component cars increased in value like the Toyota Pickup and Subaru SVX, gaining by 14% and 6%, respectively. No losses were logged while 12 others saw no change. In broad terms, aside from the ultra-exclusive LFA, the Japanese market is tracking upward at a steady, sustainable pace. It’s a good sign that what was recently an emerging hobby segment has matured. Supercar Index Broad Arrow The Hagerty Supercar Index is a stock market-style index that averages the values of 15 collectible modern supercars and hypercars. Following last quarter’s 19% increase, Hagerty’s Supercar Index continues to rise at a fast clip, rising by an additional 7%. Like with the previous quarter, the increase was largely driven by, well, everything. Of the 15 component cars, 13 posted movement, with only one of those decreasing in value. Many of the increases were in the double digit territory as well, with cars like the 2005–06 Ford GT increasing by 35%, Porsche 959 by 24%, and Ferrari F40 by 20%. Other big movers from last quarter like the Ferrari F50 and 288 GTO also continued their rise posting gains of 12% and 13%, respectively. The only decrease was the more niche Bugatti EB110, which slid by 3%. Supercars remain one of the most vibrant areas of the collector car market in 2026, and the latest update proves that last quarter was not an anomaly. If anything, things are heating up more with enthusiasm being spread to cars beyond the ones carrying Ferrari badges. We look forward to increasing the dividend while realizing strong returns as we take over the asset. We are also pleased to welcome Citizens, our RBL lender, into our ABS Warehouse Facility in conjunction with our first funding,” said Will Ulrich, Chairman and Co-CEO of Presidio. title: RTX's Pratt & Whitney Canada advances hybrid-electric technology development
summary: Ground testing of flight-standard engine and propeller for RTX Hybrid-Electric Flight Demonstrator begins in Quebec LONDON, July 21, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Farnborough International Airshow– Pratt & Whitney Canada today announced a new phase in the RTX Hybrid-Electric Flight Demonstrator project, with ground testing of the flight-standard propulsion system and propeller in Longueuil, Quebec. Following completion of the ground test, the hybrid-electric propulsion system will be installed on the De Havilland Canada Dash 8-100 experimental aircraft, with the first flight expected in 2027. Pratt & Whitney is an RTX (NYSE: RTX) business.
body_text: RTX's Pratt & Whitney Canada advances hybrid-electric technology development July 21, 2026 Share this article on Facebook Share this article on Twitter Share this article on LinkedIn Share this article via email Ground testing of flight-standard engine and propeller for RTX Hybrid-Electric Flight Demonstrator begins in Quebec LONDON , July 21, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Farnborough International Airshow – Pratt & Whitney Canada today announced a new phase in the RTX Hybrid-Electric Flight Demonstrator project, with ground testing of the flight-standard propulsion system and propeller in Longueuil, Quebec. Following completion of the ground test, the hybrid-electric propulsion system will be installed on the De Havilland Canada Dash 8-100 experimental aircraft, with the first flight expected in 2027. Pratt & Whitney is an RTX (NYSE: RTX) business. "Assembling the final, flight-standard propulsion system brings us one step closer to proving hybrid-electric technology in flight," said Jean Thomassin, executive director, New Products and Services Introduction, Pratt & Whitney Canada. "We are advancing thermal engine and hybrid-electric technologies which could enhance fuel efficiency and performance for a wide range of future aircraft applications." The hybrid-electric propulsion system combines an advanced Pratt & Whitney Canada thermal engine with a 1-megawatt electric motor and motor controller developed by RTX's Collins Aerospace, along with a battery system supplied by H55 S.A., a Swiss developer of certifiable aviation energy storage systems. With the electric motor providing additional power during demanding flight phases such as takeoff and climb, the hybrid-electric architecture enables the propulsion system to operate more efficiently throughout the flight mission. The project aims to demonstrate up to 30% improved fuel efficiency for a typical 250-nautical-mile regional turboprop mission. The RTX Hybrid-Electric Flight Demonstrator project has accelerated collaboration between leading aerospace industry companies and research institutions within Canada and abroad, including De Havilland Aircraft of Canada, GKN Aerospace, AeroTEC, Ricardo, the National Research Council of Canada and the Innovative Vehicle Institute. The project is supported by the governments of Canada and Quebec. Additionally, the project's propulsion system verification phase is supported by Strix, the organization managing Canada's Initiative for Sustainable Aviation Technology (INSAT), with funding from the Government of Canada, as part of its fifth wave of innovative research projects. Learn more about how RTX is developing transformative technologies in Canada here . The RTX Hybrid-Electric Flight Demonstrator is targeting up to 30% improved fuel efficiency on a Dash 8-100 test aircraft. title: Webflow vs WordPress in 2026: Which One Saves You More Time?
summary: A Webflow vs WordPress comparison with live August 2026 pricing, SEO and Core Web Vitals data, real maintenance hours, and the agency and enterprise trade-offs.
body_text: Key takeaways: WordPress runs 41.2% of all websites and 59.1% of the CMS market as of August 2026. Webflow runs 0.8% and 1.2%. Ubiquity is WordPress's real advantage, and it is the reason its talent pool and plugin ecosystem are unmatched. Webflow's time saving is in maintenance you never do. WordPress's time saving is in problems somebody has already solved, so you do not have to build a solution. Live pricing changed recently: Webflow Basic is $15/month billed yearly and the CMS-capable plan is now Premium at $25/month, with a new Team tier at $2,500/month. The $18/$23/$39 tiers quoted across most comparisons are stale. "WordPress" means two different products. WordPress.org is the free self-hosted software behind that 41.2%; WordPress.com is Automattic's hosted service starting at $4/month. Comparisons that mix them are comparing nothing. The honest version of this comparison is that both platforms save you time, at different moments, and the moment that matters depends on who does the work. Webflow saves the time you would have spent on updates, plugin conflicts, security patches, and the hosting stack. WordPress saves the time you would have spent building something that a plugin already does, out of the largest open-source plugin directory on the web. If you pick based on which is "better," you will pick wrong about half the time. If you pick based on which kind of time your team actually loses, you will pick right almost always. We're Awesomic, and we build on both, so this is not a pitch for one of them. We've watched a Webflow site ship in nine days and we've watched a WordPress build absorb three weeks of plugin debugging. We've also watched the reverse. What follows is the comparison with live numbers, checked in August 2026, because most of what is published about this pairing quotes pricing that no longer exists. The short answer If your team has no developer and your site is mostly marketing, Webflow will save you more time. Ask it the other way round, WordPress vs Webflow, and the answer flips as soon as your site depends on search traffic at volume, a custom content structure, ecommerce, or integrations with systems you do not control. The gap widens as the site grows. That is the whole answer. Everything below is the evidence for it and the edge cases where it flips. What Webflow is Webflow is a visual development platform: you build in a canvas that maps directly onto HTML and CSS, and it hosts the result. There is no separate hosting account, no plugin updates, and no database to maintain. Webflow's homepage, webflow.com (August 2026). The current positioning is worth noticing. The hero reads "Make your website a growth engine," the subhead promises brand building, ranking in AI search, and revenue, and the three cards below it push Enterprise, Webflow AEO, and a Webflow MCP server at version 2.0. Logos across the bottom include Spotify, Dropbox, TED, monday.com, Greenhouse, and SoundCloud. Two things follow from that. Webflow has moved firmly upmarket, and it is betting on AI search visibility as a differentiator rather than on being an easier website builder. For a marketing team, that means the product roadmap is pointed at your problems. For a developer, it means the platform is becoming more opinionated, not less. What WordPress is, and which WordPress you mean Naming which WordPress you mean is the distinction that ruins most comparisons. WordPress.org is free, open-source software you install on hosting you choose. WordPress.com is a commercial hosted service run by Automattic with its own pricing tiers. They share a name and a code lineage and almost nothing else commercially. WordPress.org's homepage, wordpress.org (August 2026). The wordpress.org homepage says exactly what the project is: "The open source publishing platform of choice for millions of websites worldwide, from creators and small businesses to enterprises." Three cards below it cover Design, Build, and Extend, and the top-right button is "Get WordPress," a download rather than a signup. That download is the whole difference. With self-hosted WordPress you own the files, the database, and the responsibility. Nobody can change your pricing, deprecate your editor, or make your editors into paid seats, and nobody will patch your site for you either. When a statistic says WordPress powers a certain share of the web, it means this one. When a comparison shows WordPress plans starting at $4 a month, it means the other one. Webflow vs WordPress pricing Pricing is where the stale numbers do the most damage, so both of these are captured from the live pages in August 2026. Webflow's pricing page with the yearly toggle active, webflow.com/pricing (August 2026). Webflow's site plans are Starter (free), Basic at $15/month billed yearly for sites that do not need a CMS, and Premium at $25/month billed yearly for content-rich sites with CMS and traffic needs. Above those sit platform plans: Team at $2,500/month with an annual contract required, and Enterprise on custom pricing. The Basic and Premium tiers carry a "Save up to 40%" yearly discount, so monthly billing costs more. WordPress.com's pricing page, wordpress.com/pricing (August 2026). Self-hosted WordPress.org is free and priced separately through your host. WordPress.com's plans, paid yearly, run Personal at $4/month with 6 GB storage, Premium at $8/month with 13 GB, Business at $25/month with 50 GB, and Commerce at $45/month. Each shows a renewal price a dollar or two higher than the promotional first-year rate, and Enterprise routes to WordPress VIP. Self-hosted WordPress is the third column, and it is the one most businesses actually run. Here is what each route really costs for a marketing site of moderate size. Route Software Hosting Typical add-ons Realistic year one Webflow Premium Included Included Apps, extra seats $300 plus workspace seats WordPress.com Business Included Included Some plugins allowed $300 to $500 Self-hosted, budget host Free $60 to $200/year Theme, SEO, forms, backups $250 to $700 Self-hosted, managed host Free $350/year and up Theme, SEO, forms, security $600 to $1,500 Webflow Team Included Included Localization, seats $30,000 plus For concrete anchors on the self-hosted line: Kinsta's entry managed plan is $35/month, or $30/month billed annually at $350 a year for one WordPress install with 10 GB storage. Yoast SEO Premium is $118.80 a year excluding VAT. Neither is required, and both are typical. The jump from Webflow's $25 plan to its $2,500 Team plan is the number that should shape an enterprise conversation, because there is nothing between them. Webflow SEO vs WordPress Webflow's SEO tooling works correctly out of the box: editable meta titles and descriptions, automatic sitemaps, clean semantic markup, 301 redirect management, and no plugin required to get any of it. Nothing is broken by default, which is more than can be said for a fresh WordPress install with the wrong theme. WordPress wins anyway once volume enters the picture, for two reasons that have nothing to do with the platform being smarter. It has purpose-built tooling for content at scale, from taxonomies and custom post types to editorial workflow plugins. And its ecosystem has solved every structured-data, internal-linking, and programmatic-page problem that a large content operation eventually hits. Performance is the honest counterweight, and here WordPress's ubiquity works against it. The HTTP Archive's Web Almanac found that WordPress origins passed all three Core Web Vitals on mobile just 40% of the time, against a 51% pass rate across all origins, and behind Duda at 73%, Squarespace at 60%, Wix at 57%, and Drupal at 56%. That gap is largely a hosting and plugin story rather than a core-software story. It is still the average outcome for real WordPress sites, though, and your site starts at the average until you spend money moving it. For a webflow seo vs wordpress decision, the split is clean. Under roughly 100 pages with a marketing-led team, Webflow is faster to get right and stays right. Above a few hundred pages with a content team publishing weekly, WordPress gives you the controls you will eventually need, provided you pay for hosting that does not undo them. Where the hours actually go Time is the question in the title, so it deserves its own accounting. The hours do not disappear on either platform; they move. Task Webflow Self-hosted WordPress Initial build, marketing site 1 to 3 weeks, no dev needed 2 to 6 weeks, dev usually needed Publishing a new landing page Minutes, by a marketer Minutes to hours, theme dependent Platform and plugin updates None, handled by Webflow 1 to 4 hours a month, ongoing Security and backups Included Host plan or plugin, plus monitoring Adding an unusual feature Custom code or an app, sometimes not possible Almost always a plugin exists Migrating away later Export is limited Full database and file export Read the last two rows together, because they are the real trade. Webflow removes recurring maintenance and adds a ceiling. WordPress removes the ceiling and adds recurring maintenance. Neither is free. The maintenance line is the one teams underestimate. One to four hours a month sounds trivial until it lands on the person who is also running your campaigns, and until the month a plugin update breaks the contact form the week of a launch. Flexibility comparison Webflow's flexibility is real inside its own model. You get genuine control of layout, typography, and interactions, and the visual canvas produces real HTML and CSS rather than an abstraction layer. What you do not get is arbitrary server-side logic, and the CMS has hard structural limits you cannot argue with. WordPress's flexibility is close to unbounded because you can write PHP and touch the database. That is also its risk profile: unbounded flexibility means unbounded ways to build something fragile, and most of the worst WordPress sites are the ones where somebody used all of it. The practical webflow vs wordpress flexibility comparison comes down to three questions. Does your site need logic that runs on a server you control? Does your content have relationships more complicated than posts, categories, and a few reference fields? Will you need to integrate with a system that has a WordPress plugin and no Webflow app? Any yes points at WordPress. Three noes point at Webflow, and you will move faster there. Webflow vs WordPress for agencies Agencies have a consideration nobody else does: the platform choice changes their revenue model, not just their build time. On Reddit , in a thread asking WordPress users who moved to Webflow how it was going, one agency owner put it plainly. The cost of Webflow is roughly what they charge clients for hosting, and they earn about £5,000 a year from that line, so moving clients across would erase it. Another commenter offered the cleanest heuristic on the page: content sites go to WordPress, marketing sites go to Webflow. Both are anecdotal, but they name the two things agencies weigh in practice. That thread surfaced a second consideration too, which is platform risk. One reply cited a Webflow pricing change making editors into paid seats as the kind of shift a client cannot opt out of without a rebuild. With self-hosted WordPress, you can change host, theme, or plugin vendor independently, and that optionality is worth something to anyone signing multi-year client relationships. The counterweight is throughput. A Webflow agency that has standardized its components can ship a marketing site substantially faster than a WordPress shop rebuilding a theme, and faster delivery at a fixed price is margin. Webflow vs WordPress for enterprises and B2B SaaS For enterprises, the decision usually gets made by procurement and security rather than by the marketing team. Webflow's own plan comparison answers that at the Enterprise tier with granular permissions, custom roles, advanced governance, secure integrations, stronger SLAs, and a dedicated account manager. Webflow has clearly built toward it, and the Team tier at $2,500/month is the entry point to that world. WordPress answers it differently, through hosting. WordPress VIP and the managed enterprise hosts provide the compliance posture, and the software stays yours. The trade is that you are assembling the enterprise guarantees from vendors rather than buying them in one contract. For webflow vs wordpress b2b saas specifically, the pattern we see most often is a split stack. Marketing site on Webflow, because the team ships pages weekly without filing tickets. Docs, changelog, and a high-volume blog on something else, frequently WordPress, because those need structure and scale that a marketing site does not. Running both is more common than either camp admits, and it is usually the right answer for a company past Series A. The one enterprise case where Webflow is clearly wrong is a site that must run inside your own infrastructure for regulatory reasons. The one where WordPress is clearly wrong is a brand team with no engineering support and a mandate to ship a new campaign page every week. How to choose without a two-week evaluation Answer four questions honestly and the choice usually makes itself. Who edits the site week to week, a marketer or a developer? A marketer working alone points at Webflow. How many pages will exist in two years? Past a few hundred, WordPress's content tooling starts earning its maintenance cost. Is organic search a primary growth channel or a secondary one? Primary favors WordPress, especially with a publishing team. Do you need something on the site that only exists as a plugin? That is a decision, not a preference. If the answers split, take the route your team can maintain without heroics. A well-run WordPress site beats a Webflow site nobody updates, and a clean Webflow site beats a WordPress install with 34 plugins and no owner. For a longer-range view that includes a third option, our Webflow, WordPress and Framer breakdown compares all three on budget, and the templates versus custom design question is worth settling before you pick a platform at all, since it changes the cost more than the platform does. Where to start Pick the platform your weekly editor can actually operate, then design for it rather than around it. The most expensive websites we see are the ones built on the right platform by someone who did not know it well. If you already know which one you want and the gap is design and build capacity, that is the part we do. Awesomic matches you with a vetted designer in up to 24 hours on a flat monthly fee with unlimited revisions, and we build on Webflow and WordPress both. The practical benefit is that the platform decision stays yours rather than being made by whoever you hired. For teams weighing a redesign or comparing this against unlimited web development , Book demo and we'll scope it against your actual page volume. One last piece of context on scale. W3Techs data from August 2026 puts WordPress at 41.2% of all websites and 59.1% of the CMS market, with Webflow at 0.8% and 1.2%. That does not make WordPress the better tool for you. It does mean that when something breaks at 2am, the answer is more likely to already exist in a forum post, and that is a form of time saving too. Whichever you pick, a new market or a new segment usually means a wave of new pages, which is worth thinking through alongside your market development strategy and the product design techniques your team already uses. Frequently asked questions Is Webflow better than WordPress for SEO? Neither is better in the abstract, but they are good at different scales. Webflow gets the technical basics right with no configuration: meta editing, automatic sitemaps, redirects, and clean markup. WordPress gives you deeper control over content structure and a much larger ecosystem for programmatic and structured-data work, which matters once you are past a few hundred pages. Performance data cuts the other way, with WordPress origins passing Core Web Vitals on mobile at 40% against a 51% average across all origins. How much does Webflow cost compared to WordPress? Webflow site plans are $15/month for Basic and $25/month for Premium, both billed yearly, with a free Starter tier and a Team plan at $2,500/month. WordPress core software is free; you pay for hosting, which runs from about $60 a year on budget shared hosting to $350 a year for a managed plan like Kinsta's entry tier, plus optional premium plugins such as Yoast SEO Premium at $118.80 a year. WordPress.com, the hosted service, starts at $4/month. For a small marketing site the two land within a few hundred dollars of each other. Can you migrate from WordPress to Webflow? Yes, and Webflow publishes a migration guide for it, but plan for a rebuild rather than a transfer. Content moves reasonably well through CSV import into Webflow's CMS; templates, plugins, and any custom functionality do not move at all and have to be re-created. Migrating in the other direction is easier, since WordPress can import most content formats and you own the destination. Treat the direction you may want to reverse later as part of the decision. Which is better for agencies managing many client sites? It depends on what you sell. Webflow's fixed monthly cost per site is close to what many agencies charge clients for hosting, so moving a book of clients across can erase a recurring revenue line, a point agency owners raise often. WordPress keeps that line and keeps your ability to change host or vendor independently. Webflow wins on build throughput for marketing sites, which is its own margin. A webflow vs wordpress for agencies comparison is really a question about whether your business bills for builds or for retainers. Do enterprises actually use Webflow? Yes, and Webflow markets to them directly, with Enterprise plans covering granular permissions, custom roles, governance, publishing workflows, and dedicated support. Its own homepage carries logos including Spotify, Dropbox, monday.com, and Greenhouse. The practical limit for webflow vs wordpress for enterprises is infrastructure control: if regulation requires the site to run inside your own environment, self-hosted WordPress on enterprise hosting is the option that can satisfy it, and Webflow is not.
